text: Maybe you're not really depressed or angry. Maybe you're hungry.
explanation:
A hungry husband can be a very short-tempered husband; the anger isn't the real problem. Many of us feel restless and empty, so we open the fridge, scroll a little longer, watch one more episode, and still feel hungry. "Why do you spend money for what is not bread, and your wages for what does not satisfy?"

Jeremiah shows the first thing to do with God's Word: "Your words were found, and I ate them, and Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart." Not "What must I do?" but eat. Feed on it until joy springs up. The enemy always goes after God's people's harvest; don't let anything steal your time in the Word.

text: "Dad, the water runs right through the basket." "Yes, son, but look how clean the basket is now."
explanation:
A farmer's boy complained that he didn't understand the Bible when he read it. His father handed him an old basket and sent him to the stream for water. Again and again it all drained out before he got back. The father pointed out that even though the basket couldn't hold the water, it had been washed clean.

You don't analyse the vitamins in every meal before you enjoy it. Read the Bible the same way. Even what you don't yet understand is cleansing you: "the washing of water by the word." Keep reading; understanding will come, and the washing happens all along.

text: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain." Paul asks, "Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or… altogether for our sakes?"
explanation:
Reading this law, you might simply see God's kindness to animals. Paul saw more: God was speaking about people, so that "he who ploughs should plough in hope." He applied it to those who sow spiritual things into others, that they shouldn't be shortchanged.

That's a key to reading the Old Testament. Don't turn it into a list of rules; look for God's love, and for what it shows you of Jesus. A God who wouldn't let a working ox go hungry isn't a tyrant. He makes sure those who labour for Him are fed.

text: "He overthrew Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, for His mercy endures forever." Every judgment holds mercy for someone.
explanation:
All twenty-six verses of Psalm 136 end with the same refrain: ki le'olam chasdo, for His lovingkindness endures forever. It's easy to say about creation and about dividing the Red Sea. But the psalmist says it even about Pharaoh's army drowning.

Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again despite repeated chances to relent. His army was charging toward Israel's families to destroy them. If someone were about to harm your child and God stopped them, you'd say, "His mercy endures forever." When you read of judgment in Scripture, look for whose side the mercy is on, and stand there.

A wealthy art collector's only son died in a war, and when the father died his priceless collection was auctioned. The first lot was a modest portrait of the son. No one bid, until the family's old servant, who had loved the boy, bought it for a few dollars. Then the auctioneer closed the sale: the will said that whoever took the son received the entire collection.

The Bible is God's photo album of His beloved Son. If you look away while He shows it, the album closes. But receive the Son, and you receive everything with Him. "He who has the Son has life," and you're a joint heir with Christ.

text: Moses veiled his face because the glory was fading. "When one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away."
explanation:
Paul calls the law engraved on stone "the ministry of death" and "the ministry of condemnation." Even it had glory, but a fading glory, and Moses covered his face so Israel wouldn't see it fade. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" is about law versus grace, not dull Bible study versus lively Bible study.

To this day a veil remains over many "when Moses is read." Turn to the Lord before you open your Bible, and the veil lifts. "We all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image." One reader stamped "PAID" on every page of Leviticus, to remember he reads it in the light of the finished work.

text: Jesus answered the Sadducees from one word: God said "I am," not "I was," the God of Abraham.
explanation:
The Sadducees denied the resurrection. Jesus quoted God at the burning bush, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob," and concluded, "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." The argument rests on the tense. Paul likewise argued from the word "Seed" being singular, pointing to Christ.

Every word of Scripture is God-breathed. In a world of edited videos and slanted stories, you're holding truth. And it's not only for pastors: Timothy knew the Scriptures from childhood, taught by his mother and grandmother, and they "are able to make you wise for salvation": healing, deliverance and wholeness included.
